chunks: And Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from al-Hasan ibn Musa al-Khashshab from Isḥāq from Jaʿfar that ʿAlī (peace be upon him) used to say:

"When the Muḥrim (person in ḥajj/ʿumrah state of consecration) slaughters the game outside the Ḥaram (sanctuary), it is a dead body (maytah); neither a Muḥil (one out of consecration) nor a Muḥrim eats it. And when the Muḥil slaughters the game inside the Ḥaram, it is a dead body; neither a Muḥil nor a Muḥrim eats it."

key_terms.الْحَرَمُ: The sacred sanctuary (specifically Mecca in this context)
key_terms.الْمُحِلُّ: Person who has exited the state of consecration
key_terms.الْمُحْرِمُ: Person in the state of ritual consecration for Hajj or Umrah
key_terms.مَيْتَةٌ: Dead body (a specific category of inedible meat in fiqh)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on eating game slaughtered by a pilgrim outside the Haram or by a non-pilgrim inside the Haram?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the specific legal status of game slaughtered in violation of ḥajj conditions, establishing it as *maytah* (dead body) regardless of whether the slaughterer is in the state of consecration (*muḥrim*) or not (*muḥil*). The ruling emphasizes that the sanctity of the *Ḥaram* and the state of *iḥrām* create distinct prohibitions, rendering the meat inedible to both parties to preserve the ritual integrity of the pilgrimage. This highlights the Shia jurisprudential focus on the precise spatial and ritual boundaries governing sacrificial acts during the holy months.
